newsitem.title: MALTA: Air Malta explores terrain for freight and passengers.
newsitem.headline: Air Malta explores terrain for freight and passengers.

text.p: Air Malta is investigating co-sharing flights to South Africa and has just extended for a year until October 1997 a contract with Balkan Air for long- haul operations to New York.
The two moves are part of what division coordinator for operations Wilfred Borg terms "exploring windows of opportunity".

They fit in with the small airline's philosophy of being "a niche market", linked with promotion of the Mediterranean island as a hub for sea-air freight operations and as a transit hub for passengers.
"We have changed from purely tourist, mainly charter, to having a predominance of scheduled flights, and now have 44 destinations," he told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday.
"About 200,000 passengers of the 1.4 million total -- or about 13 percent -- are now purely transiting Malta," he said.
Behind this switch and increased emphasis on freight is the belief that tourism, which brings around one million people a year to Malta, cannot grow much further.
"My own view is that we are close to that limit. We carry over 50 percent of the traffic... and don't want a 'destructive war' to try to increase market share," said Borg.
This month saw the introduction of a twice weekly cargo service on a Boeing 727-100 trip-leased from DHL in Brussels to operate between there and Malta.

"We are creating a hub in Brussels to where cargo from Britain and Europe is trucked and then carried by air, and in reverse. We are testing the market. Once we have established it is viable we will look at investing in a freighter aircraft."

Air Malta also see opportunities for cooperation with the island's freeport. "There is a large move among manufacturers to operate on the just-in-time' principle where the time element of transport is vital. This is a growth area," he said.
Borg said sea traffic from countries such as Japan destined for Britain could come via Malta and be transhipped into aircraft for different destinations.
Airfreight last year rose 60 percent to 7,270 tonnes on scheduled services, much of it attributable to "Air Malta's participation in the transhipment market," its annual report says.

Air Malta is feeling its way towards long haul operations, seeking to "test the market" before looking at the huge investment needed to add to its 13-strong fleet of Airbus 320- 200s, Boeing 737-300 and 737-200As, and RJ70 Avroliners.
The Balkan Air contract just extended gives it 40 to 50 block booked seats for the New York service. It is also looking at the "new Eastern Europe -- definitely an area for growth," said Borg.
But investment is daunting and "you have got to get it right first time". Except for Dubai flights, all Air Malta crew comes home each day.
"We are still considering Beirut --creating a route and excellent connections for the Middle East and Gulf."
Some 80 percent of flights are European based and Borg says the airline operates at a disadvantage with Malta being outside the European Community.

Last weekend Malta's voters elected a government opposed to EU membership but which wants a special relationship with it. This, and joining the "Third Package" system could remove what Borg terms "the disadvantage under which we operate."
In December, Air Malta starts a further operation with a new Italian airline, AZZURRAair, in which it has a 49 percent stake.

Operating out of Bergamo near Milan, with three Avro RJ85s leased from an Air Malta subsidiary, Peregrine Aviation Leasing registered this month in Ireland, AZZURRAair will fly to Rome, Turin, Zurich, Paris, Frankfurt and London City airport.

Air Malta has been profitable every year except 1974, its first year of operation. But group head of marketing, John Saliba, said costs continued to rise while fares fell. He forecast: "Our profit this year will be a little less than the previous year" -- a pre-tax figure of Lm5.9 million ($16.7million).
